content: Experiment -1 Introduction to Automata Simulation Tools • Installation and familiarization with software tools like JFLAP for automata simulation. • Basic operations: creating and running simple finite automata. Solution : - JFLAP (Java Formal Languages and Automata Package) is an interactive educational software tool used for experimenting with formal languages and automata theory. It provides a graphical interface to design, simulate, and convert computational models like finite automata, pushdown automata, and Turing machines . Below is a complete introductory guide to getting started with JFLAP, including installation steps and an overview of basic operations. 1. Installation & Setup Because JFLAP is written entirely in Java, it is cross-platform and does not require a traditional installation process. Prerequisite: Ensure that you have the Java Runtime Environment (JRE) or Java Development Kit (JDK) installed on your system. You can check this by opening your command prompt/terminal and typing java -version. Download JFLAP: Download the executable .jar file directly from the Official JFLAP Website. Running the Software: Windows/ macOS : Simply double-click the downloaded JFLAP.jar file. Linux/Terminal: Open your terminal, navigate to the folder containing the file, and run: bash java -jar JFLAP.jar 2. The JFLAP Interface When you open JFLAP, you will see a main menu listing various computational structures. Select Finite Automaton to open a blank canvas window. The window is divided into two primary sections: The Canvas: The large white drawing area where your automaton diagram is built. The Toolbar: Located at the top, containing the core construction tools: Attribute Editor (Arrow icon): Used to select, move, or configure existing states and transitions. State Creator (State icon): Places new states onto the canvas. ➡ Transition Creator (Transition icon): Draws paths between states to establish logic. Deleter (Skull or 'X' icon): Removes unwanted states or transitions. Basic Operations: Building an Automaton To learn the basic operations, let's look at how to build a simple Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) that accepts strings over the alphabet {0, 1} ending in the number "1" . Step A: Create the States Click the State Creator tool on the toolbar. Click twice on separate areas of the canvas to create two states, which JFLAP automatically names q0 and q1. Step B: Define Initial and Final States An automaton needs a distinct starting point and at least one accepting endpoint. Switch to the Attribute Editor tool. Set Initial State: Right-click on q0 and check Initial . A small triangle will appear to the left of the state. Set Final/Accepting State: Right-click on q1 and check Final (or Toggle Accept ). The state will now display a double circle. Step C: Add Transitions Click the Transition Creator tool. Self-Loop (Staying in the same state): Click on q0 and release the mouse in place. A text box will prompt you for an alphabet symbol. Type 0 and press Enter. Moving to another state: Click on q0, hold down the mouse button, drag the cursor over to q1, and release it. Type 1 in the text box and press Enter. Complete the remaining logic by adding the final two transitions: Drag from q1 back to q0 with the label 0. Create a self-loop on q1 with the label 1. 4. Running and Testing Your Automaton Once your structure is built, you can simulate how it handles input strings to verify if it works correctly. Step-by-Step Simulation: Go to the top menu bar, click Input , and select Step with Closure or Simulate . Enter a string (e.g., 0101). You can click the "Step" button to see the state turn blue as it processes each character one by one. Batch Testing (Multiple Inputs): Click Input \( \ rightarrow \) Multiple Runs . This opens a table where you can type multiple strings at once (e.g., 11, 00, 1010 ). Click Run Inputs , and JFLAP will instantly flag each string as Accept (green background) or Reject (red background) based on your automaton's design. Experiment -2 Design and Simulation of Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA) • Construct DFA for given regular languages. • Validate the DFA by inputting sample strings to check acceptance/rejection Solution Part 1 : DFA construction Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA) A Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) is a theoretical framework used to recognize regular languages. It processes an input string character by character through a precise sequence of state transitions. A formal DFA is defined as a 5-tuple (Q, ∑, δ , q0, F)\) where: [ 1 ] Q is a finite set of states. ∑ is a finite set of input symbols (alphabet). δ is the transition function Qx ∑ ➔ Q . q0 is the initial start state q0 in Q . F is the set of accepting/final states F ⊆ Q. Design Objective Construct a minimal DFA that accepts the regular languag e L = {Strings over {a, b} that sta rt with the prefix ' ab ’}. Transition Table  q0 : Initial state (waiting for first character).  q1 : State reached after processing a valid 'a'.  q2 : Final state reached after processing ' ab '. It self-loops on any subsequent input.  qd : Dead state (trap state). If the string deviates from the pattern ' ab ', it drops here and can never escape. Part 2: DFA Simulation (Python Code) The following Python script models the state transitions exactly as described in the table above an d validates custom test cases. python class DFA : def __ init __ ( self ): # Define the states and transition mapping self.start_state = "q0" self.final_states = { "q2" } # Transition function table: delta( state, symbol) -> next_state self.transitions = { "q0" : { "a" : "q1" , "b" : " qd " }, "q1" : { "a" : " qd " , "b" : "q2" }, "q2" : { "a" : "q2" , "b" : "q2" }, " qd " : { "a" : " qd " , "b" : " qd " } } def simulate ( self , input_string ): """Simulates the input string through the DFA state machine.""" current_state = self.start_state for symbol in input_string : # Handle invalid characters outside the alphabet {a, b} if symbol not in self.transitions [ current_state ]: return "REJECTED (Invalid Token)" # Transition to the next state current_state = self.transitions [ current_state ][symbol] # Check if the final state is an accepting state if current_state in self.final_states : return f"ACCEPTED (Ended in { current_state } )" else : return f"REJECTED (Ended in { current_state } )" # --- Validation and Testing Engine --- dfa_simulator = DFA() # Sample strings to validate acceptance and rejection criteria test_strings = [ " ab " , "aba" , " abbbbba " , "a" , "b" , " ba " , " aba_invalid " ] print( f" { 'Input String' :<15} | { 'Simulation Result' :<25} " ) print( "-" * 45 ) for test in test_strings : result = dfa_simulator.simulate (test) print( f" {test:<15} | {result:<25} " ) Validation Matrix : When you run the simulator, the string evaluations align with the state rules: Experiment 3: Design and Simulation of Non-Deterministic Finite Automata (NFA) • Construct NFA for various regular languages. • Convert the designed NFA into an equivalent DFA and compare their performance Solution:- Convert the following Non-Deterministic Finite Automata (NFA) to Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA)- Transition table for the given Non-Deterministic Finite Automata (NFA) is- State / Alphabet a b → q0 q0 q0, q1 q1 – *q2 *q2 – – Let Q’ be a new set of states of the Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA). Let T’ be a new transition table of the DFA. Add transitions of start state q0 to the transition table T’. State / Alphabet a b → q0 q0 {q0, q1} New state present in state Q’ is {q0, q1}. Add transitions for set of states {q0, q1} to the transition table T’. State / Alphabet a b → q0 q0 {q0, q1} {q0, q1} q0 {q0, q1, q2} New state present in state Q’ is {q0, q1, q2}. Add transitions for set of states {q0, q1, q2} to the transition table T’. State / Alphabet a b → q0 q0 {q0, q1} {q0, q1} q0 {q0, q1, q2} {q0, q1, q2} q0 {q0, q1, q2} Since no new states are left to be added in the transition table T’, so we stop. States containing q2 as its component are treated as final states of the DFA. Solution:- Draw a PDA for the CFG given below: S → aSb S → a | b | ε The PDA can be given as: P = {(q), (a, b), (S, a, b, z0), δ, q, z0, q } The mapping function δ will be: R1: δ( q, ε, S) = {(q, aSb )} R2: δ( q, ε, S) = {(q, a) | (q, b) | (q, ε)} R3: δ( q, a, a) = {(q, ε)} R4: δ( q, b, b) = {(q, ε)} R5: δ( q, ε, z0) = {(q, ε)} Simulation: Consider the string aaabb δ( q, εaaabb , S) ⊢ δ(q, aaabb , aSb ) R3 ⊢ δ( q, ε aabb , Sb ) R1 ⊢ δ ( q, aabb , aSbb ) R3 ⊢ δ( q, ε abb , Sbb ) R2 ⊢ δ ( q, abb , abb ) R3 ⊢ δ( q, bb, bb) R4 ⊢ δ ( q, b, b) R4 ⊢ δ( q, ε, z0) R5 ⊢ δ( q, ε) ACCEPT Experiment 8:- Turing Machine Design • Design and simulate a Turing machine for basic mathematical operations (e.g., addition, subtraction). • Experiment with various inputs to test Turing machine behaviour . Solution:- def simulate_turing_addition ( input_str ): # Initialize tape as a list with extra blanks at the end tape = list( input_str ) + ['B', 'B'] head = 0 state = 'q0' print( f"Initial Tape: {''.join(tape)}") print( "-" * 30) while state != ' q_halt ': current_char = tape[ head] # Visualizing the step tape_vis = "". join( tape) print( f"State : {state} | Head at index {head} ('{ current_char }') | Tape: { tape_vis }") if state == 'q0': if current_char == '1': head += 1 elif current_char == '+': tape[ head] = '1' head += 1 state = 'q1' elif state == 'q1': if current_char == '1': head += 1 elif current_char == 'B': head -= 1 state = 'q2' elif state == 'q2': if current_char == '1': tape[ head] = 'B' head -= 1 state = ' q_halt ' print( "-" * 30) print( f"Final Tape : {''.join(tape).replace('B', '')} (Result: { tape.count ('1')})") # Test with 3 + 2 simulate_turing_ addition ( "111+11")
